introduction: The Theatre Arts School-Based Assessment is practical work: your contribution to the making of a production, the documentation of that work as it developed, and a written reflection on your own practice and the performance. Depending on the requirement you may produce performance work, design or technical work, devising or writing, dance or movement work. Marks are given for the technical skill demonstrated, the research and development, the collaboration and discipline shown, and the quality of the reflection. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the structure and mark allocation required.

tasks.title: Research and preparation
tasks.explanation: Record your research into the script, period, style, cultural form or technical requirement for your chosen role, with sources, and explain how it shaped your work.

tasks.title: Development of the work
tasks.explanation: Keep a dated log of your rehearsal or construction process: exercises, experiments, drafts, blocking or plans, notes taken, problems found and changes made.

tasks.title: Production contribution
tasks.explanation: Complete the performance, design, technical, devising or movement work to which you were assigned, of a standard and detail appropriate to your role, and take part in the production itself.

tasks.title: Working in the company
tasks.explanation: Demonstrate reliability, punctuality, discipline, receptiveness to direction, safe practice and support for other members of the company, evidenced by your log and the company's records.

tasks.title: Evaluation and reflection
tasks.explanation: Evaluate your own contribution against the production's aims: what you achieved, what you would do differently, how an audience received the work, and what you learned about the art form and your role in it.

sampleTitle: Working as assistant stage manager and understudy in a school production of a Caribbean folk play

sample.body: Week 1: read the script twice and made a scene-by-scene list of every prop, entrance and cue, then met the director to check the concept (a 1950s rural Jamaican yard) and the design requirements. Week 2: built the prompt book - script pages mounted on the right with a blank cue sheet facing, marking 46 sound cues, 38 lighting cues and 12 scene changes; researched the period for the props list (enamel basin, coal pot, wooden bench, copybook) using family photographs and the National Library photographs. Week 3: attended all rehearsals and recorded blocking for the understudy role, noting entrances, exits and business in pencil; rehearsal notes issued after each session and copies given to the director and the set designer. Week 4: ran the props table with the props master, sourced and labelled 27 hand props, and ran the first props rehearsal where three props failed (the coal pot too heavy to move quietly, the basin the wrong size to fit the shelf, the copybook too small to be seen from row ten) and replacements were agreed and collected before the next rehearsal. Weeks 5-6: called the technical rehearsal cue by cue, timed each scene change, and revised the cue sheet after five changes shifted because a scene ran longer than rehearsed.
sample.tips: Write the log as you go, with dates, counts and problems. Specific records of numbers of cues, props and timings are what show real work.

sample.body: My contribution held: no cue was missed in four performances and the fastest scene change came down from 48 seconds in the first technical to 22 seconds, though that was still longer than the 15 seconds the design intended, and the audience was aware of it in the two performances where they could hear the bench being moved. The lesson is that the scene change should have been designed out, not scheduled - if the bench had been on a truck or the scene had been played in a different area, the problem would not have existed. Understudying taught me to watch the play as a whole rather than only my own moments, and the cast commented that there was no difference in the two performances I covered for a sick actor. My log broke down when I had to miss two rehearsals through illness, and I lost the running order for one scene; my improvement for next time is to have another company member briefed as a second record keeper, and to photograph and back up the prompt book weekly rather than only at the end.
sample.tips: Name one thing you would design or organise differently and one specific change you will make, and evaluate the audience's experience.

marking: Marks reward thorough research, a detailed and honest development log, practical work of a real technical standard, professional collaboration and discipline, safe practice, and a reflective evaluation that identifies what the audience experienced and what would be improved.

categories.comment: The script is analysed scene by scene (12 scene changes and 96 logged cues are listed before a single rehearsal is called), the period is researched from named sources, and each source is shown changing a decision - the copybook, the coal pot and the washing line all come from it.

A dated log runs across all ten weeks with the record kept for each week, and it reports the failures as plainly as the successes: three props failed at the first props rehearsal and were replaced, five cue numbers shifted at week 6, and the Friday backup slipped in weeks 6 and 7 and had to be caught up after the dress rehearsal.

The prompt book carries 46 sound cues, 38 lighting cues and 12 scene changes, each scene change is timed in the technical and again in every performance, and the desk was called through the technical, the dress and all four performances with no cue missed and 27 hand props labelled and tracked.

Attendance is recorded against every call (32 of 34, the two absences notified in advance and named in the log), notes were issued after each rehearsal attended, safe practice is recorded as a routine rather than a promise, and the two understudy covers for a sick actor were taken without the director changing a single piece of blocking.

The reflection evaluates the candidate's own practice and the audience's experience: it names the scene change that the audience could hear in two performances, argues that the problem should have been designed out rather than scheduled, records what the cast said about the two covers, and gives two specific changes with an owner and a date for each.

pages.heading: Cover page and contents of this Theatre Arts SBA
pages.body: This portfolio is a complete worked example of the Theatre Arts School-Based Assessment: the practical work of assistant stage managing and understudying a school production, documented as the work developed and reflected on afterwards. Theatre Arts is assessed on practical work rather than a written paper, so what follows is a portfolio and not an essay. The production was Dry River Morning, an original script written by the drama teacher and the sixth-form writers group, played as a 1950s rural Jamaican yard. My role was assistant stage manager and understudy for the role of Marcia. I was responsible for the prompt book and the cue sheet, the props table, the blocking record for my understudy part, the scene-change timings, and calling the cues from the desk at the technical, the dress and all four performances. The candidate, the school, the company, the play and every figure in this portfolio are invented for CSEC Compass, and every count, average and gap is calculated from the tables in it.

pages.heading: Research: the script, the period and what the role demanded
pages.body:
Research came first and it changed the work. The script was read twice before the first rehearsal and broken down scene by scene: 12 scene changes, 46 sound cues and 38 lighting cues were listed, with every entrance, exit, prop handle, hand-over and special effect written on the cue sheet. That list is not paperwork for its own sake. It is the reason the props table could be set up before the first props call and the reason nothing was discovered for the first time at the technical.

The period research was about the difference between a play set in a rural Jamaican yard in the 1950s and a play that only says it is. Sources were recorded as they were used, and each one is shown below with the decision it changed: the coal pot, the enamel basin, the wooden bench, the copybook, the washing line and the kerosene lamp. The oral history was the most useful source and the least convenient: forty minutes with my grandmother's neighbour, who grew up in a yard like the one in the play, produced the detail that the lamp was carried, not left on the table, which is why the lamp became a hand prop rather than set dressing.

pages.heading: Method: how the records were kept and how the work was measured
pages.body:
Method: how the records were kept and how the work was measured. Every claim in this portfolio comes from a written record, and every record was kept while the work was happening rather than written up afterwards. The prompt book is the spine of it: script pages mounted on the right, a blank cue sheet facing each page, 46 sound cues, 38 lighting cues and 12 scene changes marked in pencil so they could be revised, and the running order in the front. The props table is the second record: every one of the 27 hand props was sourced, labelled with its scene and its owner, and placed on a marked position on the table, so any missing prop was visible before a rehearsal rather than during a scene.

The measurement method matters as much as the log. Scene changes were timed from the last line of the outgoing scene to the first line of the incoming scene, using the same stopwatch and the same two timers (me, with the stage crew as the second timer) so a single slow reaction could not distort a reading. Each change was timed three times: at the first technical, at the dress, and at every performance. The times in the results table are the final-performance times, with the first-technical times beside them so the improvement is visible and so the changes that are still over target cannot hide. Attendance was recorded against every call, and the prompt book - blocking margins and all - was photographed at the Friday backup, because a pencil margin is only useful if a copy of it still exists the following week.

pages.heading: Results: every scene change timed against its design target
pages.body:
Results: every scene change timed against its design target. The design brief set a target for each change rather than one target for all of them: 15 seconds where one area of the yard was dressed and re-dressed, 20 or 25 seconds where a larger area moved, and 30 seconds where the whole playing area had to be struck. The table gives the first-technical time and the final-performance time for each of the 12 changes, with the gap to target stated in seconds rather than as a percentage, because a change that is still slow is still slow however much it improved. Across the twelve changes the average came down from 60.4 s at the first technical to 26.3 s at the closing performance, a reduction of 56.4 per cent, and 6 of the 12 changes finished inside their target. The fastest change, SC2, came down from 48 s to 22 s - a cut of 26 s, or 54.2 per cent - and it is still 7 s longer than the 15 s the design intended.

6 changes were still over target at the closing performance: SC1 by 14 s, SC2 by 7 s, SC3 by 3 s, SC6 by 5 s, SC7 by 12 s, SC10 by 13 s. Every one of them ends with furniture or set moving across the playing area in front of the audience, whereas the changes that finished inside their targets were the ones dressed within reach of the wings. That pattern is the finding of this portfolio and it is taken up in the discussion.

pages.heading: Results: the four performances, the covers and the audience
pages.body:
Results: the four performances, the covers and the audience. I called the desk at all four performances from the prompt book. No cue was missed in any of them, and the fastest scene change was never slower than 24 s, so the figures in the results table are performance figures rather than rehearsal figures. The two middle performances are the ones where I also went on for the role of Marcia, whose actor was taken ill after the opening night: the covers were called for the second night and again for the schools matinee the following morning, so the blocking notes had to be usable within a day of the call rather than within two weeks, and that is where the pencil margin earned its keep. The cast's comment in the company evaluation - that there was no difference in the two performances I covered - is the evidence I value most, because it is the only assessment of my acting in this portfolio that came from the people on stage with me rather than from me.

Audience numbers are the school's ticket records and the staff roll for the matinee, totalling 795 across the four performances. Recording them matters for the reflection rather than for the production: an audience that laughs and talks during a scene change is an audience telling you that the change is part of the play whether you wanted it to be or not, and that happened in two of the four performances.

pages.heading: Collaboration: attendance, reliability and safe practice
pages.body:
Collaboration: attendance, reliability and safe practice. Being assistant stage manager means other people cannot start until you are in place, so attendance is not a formality. I attended 32 of the 34 rehearsals called and was punctual for all 32; the two absences were notified to the director in advance, and both are in the log rather than left out of it. I issued 32 sets of rehearsal notes, one after each rehearsal I attended, and the designer used them to re-plan two costume changes.

Safe practice was recorded as a routine: cables taped and tested before each call, the lamp checked with the teacher before it was used, a no-go area marked behind the set and lit with a small floor lamp, the props table weight rule observed after the coal pot was replaced, and two-person lifts for the bench and the church pews. Nobody was injured in ten weeks and four performances, and the checklist in the log book is the record of why. On the company side, I walked the second understudy through the blocking that I had recorded, timed a scene for the designer when the sound department was short-handed, and covered the two performances at a day's notice without the director changing any blocking for the rest of the cast.

pages.heading: Discussion: what worked, what did not, and why
pages.body:
Discussion: what worked, what did not, and why. Two things worked, and both of them were decisions taken before the rehearsals started rather than during them. First, the breakdown: with 96 cues listed before the first call, the technical rehearsal was a rehearsal rather than a discovery, and no cue was missed in four performances. Second, the props table: because every one of the 27 hand props was labelled with its scene and position, the three failures at the first props rehearsal were found in week 4 rather than in week 8. The replacements - a lighter coal pot, a smaller basin, a bigger copybook - are the clearest evidence in the portfolio that the props rehearsal did its job, because a props rehearsal exists to find exactly that.

The thing that did not work was the scene changes, and the numbers say so plainly rather than being softened: 6 of 12 were still over target at the close, and every one of them involved furniture crossing the playing area in front of the audience. The audience heard the bench being moved in two performances, and although the time came down from 48 seconds to 22 seconds the change was never going to be invisible, because the problem was the design and not the crew. The honest conclusion is that the change should have been designed out rather than scheduled: with the bench on a low truck, or with the scene played in a different area of the yard so the bench did not have to move at all, the fastest change could have gone below the 15 second target instead of stopping at 22 seconds. Calling it faster was never the answer.

Two smaller failures belong in the discussion as well. I missed two rehearsals through illness in week 7 and lost the running order for one scene, and the reason I could rebuild it was that the rehearsal notes and the photographed blocking pages existed; the reason it happened was that only one person, me, was holding the record. And the Friday backup slipped in weeks 6 and 7, exactly when the cue sheet was being revised: nothing was backed up at the end of week 6, and the week 7 backup was taken late, after the dress rehearsal. It caught up before the performances, but 'it caught up' is luck, not method.
bullets: Worked: the pre-rehearsal breakdown (96 cues) - the technical was a rehearsal, not a discovery
Worked: the labelled props table - three failures found in week 4 and replaced before week 5
Did not work: 6 scene changes still over target, all of them moves in front of the audience - a design problem, not a crewing problem
Did not work: one record keeper only, and a backup schedule that slipped when the cue sheet was being revised

pages.heading: Conclusion: reflection on my practice and what I would change
pages.body:
Conclusion: what I achieved, what I would change, and what this production taught me. My contribution held: no cue was missed in four performances, 27 hand props were tracked without a single missing prop at the desk, the fastest scene change came down from 48 seconds at the first technical to 22 seconds by the closing night, and I covered the role of Marcia for 2 performances at a day's notice. Of those, the covers are the part I am most confident about and the scene changes are the part I am least confident about, and both assessments are supported by records rather than by feeling.

Two changes would improve the next production, and each has an owner and a date. First, the scene changes: the design team should review every change where furniture crosses the playing area before the set is built, with the bench either on a truck or moved out of the playing area by a scripted action, to be agreed at the design meeting in week 1 of the next production. Second, the records: a second record keeper should be briefed and named in the company list before the first rehearsal, and the prompt book should be photographed and backed up every Friday without exception, so that a week off through illness costs the production nothing. Both changes are small, and both come from a failure I can point to in my own log.

What I learned about the art form is that stage management is a way of seeing the whole play rather than a way of guarding a book. Calling the desk made me watch cues, entrances and props as one system, and understudying made me learn the play from the inside for the first time in three school productions; the two halves of the role taught me the same lesson from opposite directions, which is that the audience experiences the production's timing long before it experiences anybody's acting. The company evaluation meeting recorded the same point from the other side: the cast noticed the covers not at all and noticed the bench every time it moved.
bullets: Contribution held: 0 cues missed in four performances; 27 props tracked with none missing at the desk
Understudy covers: 2 performances at a day's notice; cast evaluation comment recorded in the company meeting notes
Change 1: design review of every change where furniture crosses the playing area, agreed at the week 1 design meeting
Change 2: a named second record keeper, and the prompt book photographed and backed up every Friday without exception

pages.heading: Sources and honesty note for this worked example
pages.body:
Every name, school, company member, date, cue count, prop and timing in this portfolio is invented for CSEC Compass. The play, Dry River Morning, is an invented script and its author is invented; the candidate, the centre, the director, the cast, the crew and the oral-history source are all invented, and the audience figures and ticket records are invented with them. Nothing here is taken from another candidate's portfolio, from a real school production, from a published play, or from any examination material, and no text has been reproduced from any source. Every count, average, percentage and gap in the tables is calculated from the records shown in the portfolio itself, so the portfolio can be checked against itself.

The purpose of the sample is to show the shape of a strong Theatre Arts portfolio: a role defined in writing before the work starts, a dated log that keeps the failures in it, records kept while the work is happening rather than written up afterwards, timings measured the same way every time and reported with the targets beside them, a company record of attendance and safe practice, and a reflection that names the production's weakest moment, explains why it was a design problem rather than a crewing problem, and commits to two specific changes with owners. Use it for the method: define the role, keep the log as you go, measure what you claim, and report what did not work as plainly as what did.
bullets: All names, dates, records, figures and the play itself are invented for this sample; nothing reproduced from any source
Every derived figure calculated from the tables: the 56.4 per cent average improvement, the 6 changes still over target, the audience total of 795
Reusable method: role in writing, dated log with failures kept in, timings measured the same way each time, targets shown beside the results

examinerNotes: Practical work is evidenced in numbers rather than in adjectives: 46 sound cues, 38 lighting cues and 12 scene changes logged before the first rehearsal, every scene change timed at the technical, the dress and all four performances, and no cue missed in any of them.

The three props that failed at the first props rehearsal are recorded with the replacement agreed for each, which is what a props rehearsal is for; the portfolio shows the failure and the fix rather than only the finished table.

The reflection is candid and specific: it reports that 6 scene changes were still over target, names the audience hearing the bench in two performances, and concludes that the change should have been designed out rather than called faster, which is the judgement the Reflection marks are awarded for.

Collaboration is evidenced by records rather than by claims: 32 of 34 rehearsals attended with both absences notified in advance, 32 sets of notes issued, a signed safe-practice checklist, and 2 understudy covers taken at a day's notice.
